J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. In this appeal, the Appellant has assailed the order dated 2nd
February, 2021 passed by the 1st Respondent – Tamil Nadu Electricity
Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”) in
DRP No. 7 of 2020 filed by the Appellant thereby refusing to grant project
specific extension of the Commercial Operation Date (COD) of the
Appellant’s solar power project. The Commission has also held that since
the Appellant’s power project was not commissioned within 22 months
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 2 of 20

from 22nd March, 2018 (date of signing of the PPA between it and the 2nd
Respondent), the PPA stood automatically terminated and the 2nd
Respondent is entitled to relief provided under Article use 14 of the PPA
to the extent of non-commissioning of the power project by the Appellant.
2. The Appellant is a company registered under Companies Act, 2013
and is engaged in the business of solar power generation as well as other
allied activities.
3. Respondent No. 2 – Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution
Corporation Limited (TANGEDCO) is the sole distribution licensee in the
State of Tamil Nadu.
4. Brief facts of the case, relevant for the disposal of the instant
appeal, are that 2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO issued a tender in the
year 2017 for procurement of total capacity of 1500 MW of solar power
from the developers on long-term basis. The tender was prepared and
issued in line with the “Guidelines for tariff based competitive bidding
process for procurement of power from grid connected solar PV power
projects, 2017” dated 3rd August, 2017 issued by the Ministry of Power,
Government of India as a guiding principle.
5. The Appellant also participated in the tender and was declared L-1
bidder. Accordingly, Letter of Intent (LOI) dated 2nd January, 2018 was
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 3 of 20

issued by 2nd Respondent to the Appellant. As required under clause 5.0
of the LOI, the Appellant furnished two Performance Bank Guarantees
for a total amount of Rs.10 crores and also entered into Power Purchase
Agreement dated 22nd March, 2018 with the 2nd Respondent –
TANGEDCO for a period of 25 years.
6. As per clause 14 of the PPA, the Appellant had to commission its
power project by 21st March, 2019 i.e. within 12 months from the date of
the signing of the PPA.
7. Subsequent to signing of the PPA, the Appellant finalized its
location for its solar power project at Vilathikulam Tuticorim District, Tamil
Nadu and purchased the site land and also registered the same in its
name on 26th April, 2018. Immediately, thereafter, the Appellant
commenced the ground work for establishing the power project i.e.
cleaning of land, bush removal etc.
8. The Appellant communicated its acceptance of LOI on 25th July,
2018 and at the same time requested for change of location of the power
project from Virudhunagar District (as identified earlier by the Appellant)
to Vilathikulum Taluk, which request was accepted by 2nd Respondent –
TANGEDCO. Accordingly, a certificate in this regard was issued to the
Appellant certifying that the solar plant can be interfaced to Vilathikulum
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 4 of 20

110/33-11 KV SS at 110 KV level through a dedicated 110 KV power
evacuation line.
9. Vide notification dated 30th July, 2018, the Ministry of Finance
imposed a “Safeguard Duty” (in short “SGD”) on the modules and solar
panels to be imported from all developed countries such as China,
Taiwan and Malaysia. The notification imposed safeguard duty beyond
25% on the advolerum value of the modules thereby increasing the price
of modules by 25%.
10. The Ministry of Power, Government of India took note of the impact
of the levy of SGD upon the upcoming solar power projects and
accordingly issued under Section 107 of the Electricity Act to the Central
Commission on 21st August, 2018 stating that the solar power generators
can be duly compensated as a pass through for sudden levy of SGD as
the same amounts to a change in law situation.
11. The Cyclone Gaja accompanied by heavy rains are stated to have
hit the coast of Tamil Nadu in December, 2018 due to which Appellant’s
project was severely affected. There was severe water logging at the site
and the Appellant has to restart the preliminary work that had already
been completed. This severely impacted the viability of the entire project
of the Appellant and resulted in an increased overall project cost by 17%.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 5 of 20

12. Accordingly, Appellant wrote a letter dated 18th December, 2018 to
2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO stating these reasons and seeking an
extension of the Scheduled Commercial Operation Date (SCOD) of the
power project by four months i.e. from 21st March, 2019 to 21st July, 2019.
However, the TANGEDCO rejected the said request of the Appellant vide
letter dated 7th January, 2019 stating that as per the commercial schedule
in the tender specification, the Appellant could commission the project on
or before 21st January, 2020 subject to the conditions mentioned therein.
13. A memorandum of understanding is stated to have been executed
between the Appellant and the Government of Tamil Nadu represented
by TANGEDCO on 24th January, 2019 during Global Investor Meet
whereby TANGEDCO agreed to provide infrastructural and regulatory
support to facilitate the project in view of substantial investment being
made by the Appellant. In view of the assurances, the Appellant placed
two purchase orders dated 6th February, 2019 and 10th February, 2019
upon M/s DK Solar Projects & Ventures Pvt. Ltd. for a complete EPC
package for 53 MWp solar power project and for sub-station
components.
14. At the same time, TANGEDCO addressed the communication
dated 3rd September, 2019 to the Appellant as well as to the bankers of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 6 of 20

the Appellant seeking to invoke the Performance Bank Guarantee
furnished by the Appellant to the tune of Rs.10 crores citing the delay in
commissioning of the project. Thereafter, the Performance Bank
Guarantee for a sum of Rs.5.10 crores was encashed by TANGEDCO
on 7th September, 2019 to which the Appellant strongly objected.
15. Vide letter dated 27th October, 2019, the Appellant requested
TANGEDCO to refrain from forfeiting the Performance Bank Guarantee
furnished by it with further request to allow the Appellant to complete the
project by 26th June, 2020. However, no response was received by the
Appellant to the said communication.
16. Vide letter dated 5th December, 2019, the Respondent No. 3 denied
Appellant’s request for extension of COD and stating that the Appellant
was required to furnish the commissioning of the power plant by 21st
January, 2020. Vide another letter dated 20th December, 2019,
Respondent No. 3 directed the Appellant to furnish a fresh Performance
Bank Guarantee to a tune of Rs.7.60 crores for the delay of five months
in commissioning of the project.
17. Feeling aggrieved by the refusal of the 2nd Respondent –
TANGEDCO in granting the extension of SCOD of the power project or
approving the part commissioning of the project despite Appellant having
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 7 of 20

taken active steps to complete the project and having expressed
willingness to perform its obligations under the PPA, the Appellant
approached the Commission by way of the petition being DRP No. 7 of
2020 seeking following prayers :-
“a) Grant the Petitioner a project specific extension of the COD
by eighteen months i.e. 21.3.2019 to 21.9.2020 in respect of the
Petitioner's SPG under PPA dated 22.03.2018 and
consequently quash the letters dated 05.12.2019.
b) Direct the 1st and 2nd Respondents not to enforce any
security including bank guarantees and allow for its
continuance pending disposal of this petition upon such terms
as the Commission may deem fit in the facts and circumstances
of the case; and
c) Direct the 1st and 2nd Respondent to repay a sum of
Rs.5,10,00,000/ collected under Bank Guarantee dated
21.03.2018 in order that the Petitioner cam reinstate such bank
guarantee and keep it alive in terms of the PPA dates
22.03.2018 and upon such terms as the Commission deems
fit.”
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 8 of 20

18. The petition has been disposed of by the Commission vide the
order dated 2nd February, 2021 which has been impugned in this appeal.
The Commission vide the impugned order, has not only refused to grant
extension of COD to the power project of the Appellant but has also held
that the PPA stood terminated automatically as the Appellant did not
commission the power project within the stipulated 22 months from the
date of signing of the PPA and also held the Respondent – TANGEDCO
entitled to invocation of the Performance Bank Guarantee submitted by
the Appellant as well as the liquidated damages as provided under clause
14 of the PPA.
19. We have heard Shri Aditya Singh, Learned Counsel for the
Appellant and Ms. Anusha Nagarajan, Learned Counsel for Respondent
Nos. 2 to 5. We have also perused the written submissions filed by the
Learned Counsel.
20. From the submission of the Learned Counsel for the Appellant, it
appears that the primary grievance of the Appellant is that the
Commission, in the impugned order, has over-looked the impact of the
cyclone and heavy rain on the development of the power project as
contended by the Appellant in its pleadings. It is argued that neither is
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 9 of 20

there discussion on this aspect in the entire impugned order nor have
any findings been returned by the Commission on the same.
21. We note that the Appellant had specifically pleaded in paragraph
No. 23 of the petition filed before the Commission that its project was
severely affected by unforeseen natural disaster i.e. cyclone that hit the
cost of Tamil Nadu during the month of November, 2018. In paragraph
No. 29 of the petition, the Appellant had stated that it wrote two letters to
the Respondents seeking extension of COD of the power project on the
ground of natural disaster and low bank credit rating of TANGEDCO.
These paragraphs of this petition are extracted hereinbelow :-
"23. The Petitioner submits that vide letter dated
18.12.2018, the Petitioner intimated to the 2nd
Respondent that due to the unforeseen natural disaster
that hit the coast Of Tamil Nadu during November, 2018,
the Petitioner's project was severely affected and the
Petitioner was set back in project development by four
months. In light of the same, the Petitioner sought COD
extension by 4 months, i.e. from 21.03.2019 to
21.07.2019. TO this letter, the 2nd Respondent
TANGEDCO replied stating that the Petitioner had time
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 10 of 20

till 21-01.2020 to commission its power plant, as per the
PPA dated 22.03.2018, during Which time the
TANGEDCO will be entitled to invoke the bank guarantee
for every day's delay.
29. The petitioner wrote two letters to the Respondent
Seeking extension COD on the ground of natural disaster
and low bank credit rating of TANGEDCO by the
Petitioner dated 18.12.2018 and 22.10.2019. However,
the Petitioner has received response from the
Respondent dated 07.01.2019 and 05.12.2019, in which,
the Respondent denied the extension of COD stating not
feasible."
22. The 2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO had in paragraph No. 29 of its
reply to the petition referred to and responded to these assertions of the
Appellant. The said paragraph of the reply of TANGEDCO filed before
the Commission is extracted hereinbelow :-
"29. It is respectfully submitted that the petitioner in para
23 of its petition has stated that they have been prevented
from developing and commissioning the solar power plant
at Tuticorin district because of natural disaster that hit the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 11 of 20

coast of Tamil Nadu in November 2018. Further 5
developers have commissioned solar power plants of
combined capacity of 500 MW within scheduled date of
commissioning at Tuticorin district under this scheme and
they have not claimed any time extension due to the
reasons stated above by the petitioner company. Hence
the reason stated by the petitioner is not acceptable and
justifiable and such a reason is stated to cover up his
commissions and omissions in pursuing the contract
conditions."
23. In paragraph No. 7 of the rejoinder filed by the Appellant, it
reiterated its assertions with regards to the complete inundation of the
project site due to heavy rains that had hit the coast of Tuticorim in
November, 2018. The said paragraph of the rejoinder is extracted
hereinbelow:-
"7. Further, the Respondent has failed to consider that in
November 2018, when heavy rains hit the coast of
Tuticorin, the Petitioner's project site was completely
inundated owing to which the Petitioner's personnel were
unable to access the project site. The Respondent has
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 12 of 20

not taken cognizance of the fact that the Petitioner's
project site consists of black cotton soil which is more
susceptible to rain water stagnation, consequently, due to
the stagnation, the Petitioner was unable to carry out any
work. The contention of the Respondent that the other
developers have not cited the heavy rains to seek
extension of time is misplaced in as much as the
Respondent has failed to take cognizance of the nature
and location of the project site, which are facts peculiar
and unique to the Petitioner's project. Pertinently, in
response to the Petitioner's letter dated 18.12.2018,
seeking an extension of time for delay owing to the above
mentioned unforeseen rain and cyclone, the Respondent
has categorically stated in its letter dated 7.01.2019 that
the Petitioner had time until 21.01.2020 to commission
the power plant. Further, the 2nd Respondent had also
reiterated that the Petitioner had time till 21.01.2020, to
commission the project, in its letter dated 05.12.2020.
That being so, the Respondent cannot at this juncture
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 13 of 20

retract its stand and claim that the PPA had terminated on
21.08.2019."
24. In paragraph No. 3.10 of the impugned order, the Commission has
taken note of these averments of the Appellant contained in the petition.
The said paragraph of the impugned order is reproduced hereinbelow:-
“3.10. Vide letter dated 18.12.2018, the Petitioner intimated
to the 2nd Respondent that due to the unforeseen natural
disaster that hit the coast of Tamil Nadu during December,
2018, the Petitioner's project was severely affected and the
Petitioner suffered set back in project development by four
months and sought COD extension by 4 months, i.e. from
21.03.2019 to 21.7.2019. To the same, the 2nd Respondent
TANGEDCO replied stating that the Petitioner had time till
21.01.2020 to Commission its power plant, as per the PPA
dated 22.03.2018, during which time the TANGEDCO
would be entitled to invoke the bank guarantee for every
day's delay.”
25. The response of the TANGEDCO to these averments of the
Appellant have been noted in paragraph No. 4.26 of the impugned order
which is reproduced hereinbelow:-
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 14 of 20

“4.26. The petitioner in para 23 of its petition has stated
that it has been prevented from developing and
commissioning the solar power plant at Tuticorin district
because of natural disaster that hit the coast of Tamil
Nadu in December 2018. Further 5 developers have
commissioned solar power plants of combined capacity
of 500 MW within scheduled date of commissioning at
Tuticorin district under this scheme and they have not
claimed any time extension due to the reasons stated
above by petitioner company. Hence the reason stated by
the petitioner is not acceptable and justifiable and such a
reason is stated to cover up its commissions and
omissions in pursuing the contract conditions.”
26. We have minutely perused the entire impugned order of the
Commission. At no place in the order has the Commission discussed the
impact of cyclone and heavy rains on the development of the power
project of the Appellant. As such no findings have been returned by the
Commission on this aspect in the order. In fact, we may, record that the
findings of the Commission contained in paragraph No. 6 of the impugned
order begin with paragraph No. 6.1, contents of which indicate that the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 15 of 20

Commission has proceeded to discuss and examine the assertions of the
Appellant only with regards to the imposition of safeguard duty by the
Ministry of Finance, Government of India. The said paragraph of the
impugned order is extracted hereinbelow :-
“6.1. The instant petition is being filed seeking an
extension of the date of Commissioning (COD) by 18
months from 21-03-2019 to 21-09-2020 in respect of the
Petitioner's 50 MW power plant in respect of which the
Petitioner entered into a power purchase agreement
(PPA) dated 22.03.2018 with the 1st Respondent herein
due to a substantial change in law in respect of levy of
Safeguard Duty (SGD) by the Ministry of Finance,
Government of India and also to direct the 1st and 2nd
respondent to repay a sum of Rs.5,10,00,000/- collected
under Bank Guarantee dated 21-03-2018 in order that the
petitioner can reinstate such bank guarantee and keep it
alive in terms of the PPA dated 22-03-2018.”
27. We are unable to understand as to how the Commission chose not
to discuss the impact of the cyclone and the consequently heavy rains
upon the progress of the power project of the Appellant despite their
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 16 of 20

being ample pleadings before it in this regard. Therefore, the impugned
order is not only erroneous but also atrocious as it fails to dwell upon and
address one of the primary grievance with which the Appellant has
approached the Commission.
28. The Commission had even framed four issues for its consideration,
one of which related to the scope of Force Majeure and is extracted
hereinbelow:-
“Whether there has been a substantial change in law
which falls within the scope of Force Majeure as
contemplated under clause 16 of the PPA?”
29. In the discussion under the said issue, the Commission has
referred to and discussed only the impact of the levy of the safeguard
duty by the Central Government and has held that such levy does not fall
within the Force Majeure clause of the PPA. There is no reference to the
cyclone and the consequential heavy rains in the entire discussion under
this issue which also had been projected by the Appellant as Force
Majeure event affecting the progress of the power project.
30. Once, a statement of facts is made in the petition by the petitioner
upon which the relief claimed in the petition is founded, the same having
been denied in the reply of the respondent and re-affirmed by the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 17 of 20

petitioner in the rejoinder, the Commission was bound to take note of the
same, discuss the same and return its findings on the same in the final
order by which the petition is disposed of. In the instant case, the
Commission has completely over-looked issue of cyclone and
consequential rainfall as agitated by the Appellant as a ground for
claiming extension of SCOD of the power project. Such non-
consideration of one of the material issue in the impugned order is merely
reflects failure on the part of the Commission to properly adjudicate the
disputes between the parties, which has rendered the impugned order
unsustainable and liable to set aside.
31. The fact that Commission has passed the impugned order in a
cavalier fashion without application of mind to the contractual provisions,
is evident from bare reading of paragraphs 6.17.11 and 6.17.12 of the
order in which the Commission has extracted and discussed clause 14
of PPA of some other project developers and not of the PPA executed
between the Appellant and TANGEDCO in this case. In fact, concluding
paragraph No. 6.17.13 of the impugned order also refers to the timelines
of some other PPA and not the timelines specified in the PPA executed
in this case being a party. This factual mis-match also renders the
impugned order unsustainable and liable to set aside.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 18 of 20

32. We refrain from returning any findings on the issue of entitlement
of TANGEDCO to encash the Bank Guarantee submitted by the
Appellant and the liability of the Appellant to pay liquidated damages to
TANGEDCO, as directed by the Commission in the impugned order, as
any decision of these two issues would depend upon the findings to be
returned by the Commission with regards to the impact of Force Majeure
event i.e. cyclone along with consequential heavy rains upon the
construction of the power project of the Appellant.
33. Having regard to above discussion, we are unable to sustain the
impugned order of the Commission and the same is hereby set aside.
The case is remanded back to the Commission for fresh consideration
with regards to the impact of cyclone and the consequential heavy rains
that are stated to have hit the coast of Tamil Nadu in November, 2018,
upon the progress of the power project by the Appellant as a Force
Majeure event as contemplated under clause 16 of the PPA executed
between the parties as also upon the consequential issues related to
entitlement of TANGEDCO for encashing the Bank Guarantees
submitted by the Appellant and liability of the Appellant to pay liquidated
damages to TANGEDCO. The Commission shall render its fresh decision
after affording reasonable opportunity of hearing to all the parties and
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 214 of 2021 Page 19 of 20

while keeping in mind the observations of this Tribunal in the judgement
dated 29th July, 2026 in Appeal No. 151 of 2021 which also had arisen in
almost similar factual context and identical order passed by the
Commission. Needless to say that the Commission shall endure to pass
fresh order within three months from the date of receipt of this judgement.
Pronounced in the open court on this 31st day of July, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

O R D E R
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The review petitioner M/s SEIL Energy India Limited (formerly known
as Sembcorp Energy India Limited) has sought review of common judgment
dated 11.04.2019 passed by this Tribunal in appeal nos.363/2017 and
16/2018. Appeal no.16/2018 had been filed by the review petitioner against
the order dated 30.10.2017 passed by the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission in its petition no.240/MP/2016, whereas appeal no.363/2017
had been filed by M/s GMR Warora Energy Limited against the order dated
17.10.2017 passed by the Central Commission in its petition
no.153/MP/2016.
2. A bird’s eye view of the facts in both these appeals, which are relevant
for deciding the instant review petition, are that the review petitioner entered
into bulk power transmission agreement for Long Term Access (LTA) on
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 2 of 18

24.12.2010 for supply of 500MW power from its super critical coal fired power
plant in District Nellore, Andhra Pradesh. The Power Grid Corporation of
India Limited (in short PGCIL) respondent no.2 herein, was required to
operationalize the LTA by January, 2014. Since the review petitioner entered
into Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) on 01.04.2013 and the two units of
its power plant were commissioned on 02.03.2015 and 15.09.2015
respectively by which date LTA had not been operationalized, it applied for
Medium Term Open Access (MTOA) on 30.07.2015. MTOA was granted to
it by PGCIL on 10.09.2015. Subsequently, PGCIL intimated the review
petitioner about operationalization of LTA on 21.06.2016. Vide letter dated
09.08.2016, review petitioner sought confirmation from PGCIL whether its
MTOA had already stood terminated/downsized on account of
operationalization of LTA and further asked for relinquishment of MTOA in
case such termination had not taken place. However, vide letter dated
06.09.2016, PGCIL informed the review petitioner about acceptance of its
request for relinquishment of MOTA and also declined the request for non-
applicability of relinquishment charges in respect of relinquishment of MTOA.
Therefore, PGCIL raised PoC bill for the month of August, 2016 demanding
Rs.8,94,56,167/-(Rupees eight crores ninety four lakhs fifty six thousand one
hundred sixty seven only) from the review petitioner towards transmission
charges under the CERC (Sharing of Inter State Transmission Charges and
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 3 of 18

Losses) Regulations, 2010 (hereinafter referred to as the 2010 Sharing
Regulations). Aggrieved by the decision of PGCIL to double charge it (i.e. for
LTA Charges as well as MTOA relinquishment charges), the review
petitioner approached the Commission by way of petition no.240/MP/2016
which was disposed of vide order dated 30.10.2017 whereby the
Commission held review petitioner bound to pay
relinquishment/transmission charges for the termination of MTOA. This
order of the Commission was assailed by the review petitioner before this
Tribunal in appeal no.16/2018.
3. In so far as M/s GMR Warora Energy Limited (appellant in appeal
no.363/2017) is concerned, it had participated in the tender floated by
TANGEDCO, a distribution licensee in the State of Tamil Nadu, in the year
2012 for procurement of power on Long Term basis and was declared
successful bidder on 30.10.2013 for supply of 150MW of power.
Accordingly, PPA dated 27.11.2013 was executed between TANGEDCO
and GMR Warora for supply of 150MW of power w.e.f. 01.06.2014 for a
period of 14 years. Subsequently, GMR Warora applied to PGCIL for grant
of LTA for the said quantum of 150MW in the Southern Region for onward
supply to TANGEDCO. At the same time GMR Warora also applied for grant
of MTOA for 150MW in Southern Region. On 27.07.2015, GMR Warora
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 4 of 18

received letter from PGCIL informing it that notional LTA was granted in
pursuance to the meeting dated 15.07.2015. The LTA was for a period from
01.04.2015 to 30.09.2028.
4. On 24.07.2015 GMR Warora received a letter from PGCIL asking it to
open a Letter of Credit of Rs.901.03 lakhs with respect to the MTOA dated
22.07.2015. Thereafter, MTOA agreement was executed by GMR Warora
with PGCIL on 04.08.2015. In pursuance to the grant of LTA dated
22.07.2015, GMR Warora executed an LTA agreement dated 11.08.2015
with PGCIL. Vide letter dated 18.08.2015, PGCIL informed GMR Warora
that LTA was expected to be operationalized by October, 2015 subject to
fulfilment of conditions mentioned in the intimation for grant of LTA and
payment of relinquishment charges corresponding to 150MW MTOA.
Thereafter, PGCIL further informed GMR Warora that LTA would be
operationalized w.e.f. 22.01.2016 and also rejected its request for not
claiming relinquishment charges towards stoppage of MTOA. Vide letter
dated 09.06.2016, PGCIL raised a demand upon GMR Warora towards
payment of Rs.2,14,71,750/- as relinquishment charges for closure of MTOA
dated 22.07.2015. Aggrieved by the same, GMR Warora approached the
Commission by way of petitionno.153/MP/2016 which was dismissed by the
Commission vide order dated 17.10.2017. This order of the Commission
was impugned by GMR Warora in appeal no.363/2017.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 5 of 18

5. As already noted hereinabove, both these appeals were disposed of
by this Tribunal vide common judgment dated 11.04.2019, which is under
review, thereby affirming the impugned orders dated 17.10.2017 and
30.10.2017 of the Central Commission. The said judgment of this Tribunal
was assailed by the review petitioner in the Hon'ble Supreme Court by way
of Civil Appeal No.5169/2019 which came to be dismissed vide order dated
15.07.2019. However, liberty was given to the review petitioner to approach
this Tribunal for non-consideration of any issue raised by it in the said
judgment dated 11.04.2019 and also the finding recorded in the same that
review petitioner had agreed to pay the relinquishment charges. The said
order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court is extracted hereinbelow: -
“ORDER
Having heard learned counsel for the appellant and on
perusing the relevant material, we are not inclined to interfere.
The civil appeal is accordingly dismissed.
However, if the appellant is aggrieved by the non-
consideration of any issue raised by it and the finding recorded
by the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity that the appellant had
agreed to pay the relinquishment charges is factually incorrect
it will be open for the appellant to move the Appellate Tribunal
for Electricity once again.”
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 6 of 18

6. Accordingly, the instant review petition has been filed by the review
petitioner.
7. We have heard Shri Sajan Poovayya, learned senior counsel
appearing for the review petitioner and Ms. Ranjitha Ramachandran, learned
counsel for the 3rd respondent CTUIL. We have also perused the written
submissions filed by the learned counsels.
8. The primary ground on which the instant review petition is founded is
that this Tribunal, in the “Analysis” part of the judgment dated 11.04.2019,
has considered and discussed only the facts related to the appeal
no.363/2017 (filed by GMR Warora) and the facts involved in petitioner’s
appeal no.16/2018 have not been referred to at all. It is argued that the
review petitioner was constrained to apply for MTOA for the reason that LTA
granted to it had not been operationalized by the time it entered into PPA
with Andhra Pradesh discoms and two units of its power plant were
commissioned whereas GMR Warora had applied for both LTA as well as
MTOA simultaneously which makes its case distinct from the case of the
petitioner.
9. It is further argued on behalf of the petitioner that GMR Warora had
given a specific consent for payment of relinquishment charges vide its letter
dated 13.01.2016 sent to PGCIL, which has been relied upon by this Tribunal
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 7 of 18

while dismissing the appeal but no such undertaking had been given by the
petitioner. The submission is that the judgment under review has been
rendered in the facts and circumstances unrelated to the petitioner and is
based upon the undertaking/acceptance given by GMR Warora, not by the
petitioner, and therefore, the same cannot be applied to the petitioner’s case.
10. Thus, it is contended that the judgment dated 11.04.2019 suffers a
patent error which makes it unsustainable qua the review petitioner and calls
for rectification of those factual errors.
11. The review petition is vehemently contested on behalf of the 3rd
respondent CTUIL. It is argued that though there is slight variation between
the facts involved in the two appeals yet that was too insignificant to be taken
to differentiate the case of petitioner from that of GMR Warora. It is argued
that in essence, both the petitioner as well as GMR Warora were aggrieved
by levy of relinquishment charges for relinquishment of MTOA upon
operationalization of LTA in their favour, which aspect has been discussed
and decided in the judgment under review. It is further submitted that the
fact that petitioner has not consented to pay the relinquishment charges, as
was done by GMR Warora, was not relevant at all for the reason that this
Tribunal has reached the final conclusion upon perusal of the relevant
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 8 of 18

regulations as well as the facts involved in the two appeals de hors any such
consent given by GMR Warora.
12. It is, thus, argued that the judgment dated 11.04.2019 does not suffer
from any error apparent on the face of record and the review petition merits
dismissal.
Our Analysis: -
13. In both the above noted appeals, the appellants had challenged the
levy of relinquishment charges on them upon relinquishment of the
respective MTOAs when LTA granted in their favour were operationalized by
the 2nd respondents. However, there appears clear distinction between the
facts of the two appeals even though the relief claimed was identical.
14. Perusal of the judgment under review does reveal that it notes the facts
involved in appeal no.16/2018 (filed by petitioner herein) and the contentions
of the appellant in Paragraph nos.3.2 to 3.26. The submissions of the
petitioner’s counsel have been noted in Paragraph nos.4.1 to 4.22.
However, in Paragraph no.6.0 which precedes the “Consideration and
Analysis” part of the judgment, this Tribunal has observed that the
issues/facts as well as the submissions in appeal no.363/2017 alone are
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 9 of 18

being taken up for the sake of brevity. We find it apposite to extract the said
Paragraph of the judgment hereunder: -
“6.0 The issue and facts of the case and the submissions
of the Appellant and the Respondents in Appeal No. 363
of 2017 are similar to that in Appeal No. 16 of 2018, except
for the dates of various orders and, therefore, for the sake
of brevity we shall take up the issue and facts of the case
and the submissions of Appeal No. 363 of 2017 and,
therefore, a common judgment is being rendered.”
15. In the “Consideration and Analysis” part of the judgment, the Tribunal
has referred to the relevant regulations i.e. CERC Open Access Regulations,
2004 under which the concept of LTA and STOA was evolved as well as the
CERC Open Access Regulations, 2009 wherein the concept of MTOA
evolved. Thereafter, in Paragraph 7(vii), Regulation 24 of the CERC Open
Access Regulations, 2009 has been extracted which makes provision for
relinquishment of MTOA.
16. Subsequent Paragraph nos.7(viii), 7(ix), 7(x) and 7(xi) of the judgment
are very material and are extracted herein below: -
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 10 of 18

“viii) In the meeting for processing of LTA and MTOA
applications held on 15.7.2015, the Appellant requested
for grant of MTOA as per the application made in the
month of November, 2013 and it would relinquish MTOA
rights and pay the applicable relinquishment charges in
line with the Commission’s regulations as and when the
LTA for the application made in December, 2013 is
operationalized. Relevant portion of minutes of meeting
dated 15.7.2015 is extracted as under:
“11.0 CTU stated that GMR EMCO Energy Ltd. has
applied MTOA for 150 MW in Nov, 2013 and also
applied LTA for 150 MW in Dec, 2013 and enclosed
same PPA in both the referred applications. Towards
this, the representative of GMR stated that as per the
directions given in the CERC order, the applications
shall have to be processed sequentially i.e. the
MTOA application of Nov, 2013 shall have higher
priority than the LTA application received in Dec,
2013. He accordingly requested that MTOA may be
granted as per their applications made in the month
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 11 of 18

of Nov‟2013 and they shall relinquish MTOA rights
and pay the applicable relinquishment charges in line
with the CERC regulations as and when the LTA for
the application made in Dec ‟2013 is
operationalized.”
ix) The liability to bear charges for relinquishment of
MTOA under Regulation 24 was also a condition of the
LTA intimation dated 22.7.2015 issued by PGCIL which
contained the following condition:
“As decided in the meeting held on 15.7.2015 for
processing of pending LTA & MTOA applications received
in Nov' 13 & Dec' 13, the above grant of LTA shall not be
operationalized until the earlier granted MTOA of 150 MW
for the same PPA against the application made in Nov' 13
is relinquished.”
x) The Appellant vide its letter dated 13.1.2016 requested
PGCIL to operationalize 150 MW LTA by foreclosing the
corresponding 150 MW under MTOA and gave consent
for payment of relinquishment charges as per the
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 12 of 18

applicable regulations, rules and guidelines. The said
letter is extracted as under:
“We are in receipt of your letter dated 30th December,
2015 (Ref No. 8 above) received by us on 08.01.2016,
wherein you had sought our consent for payment of
relinquishment charges prior to operationalization of the
LTA of 150 MW. We would like to reiterate that vide our
letter dated 17th December, 2015 we had only sought for
conversion of our MTOA of 150 MW to LTA of 150 MW for
purpose of meeting our commitment for supply of power
to TANGEDCO on long term basis. As such there is no
relinquishment of open access capacity of 150 MW per se
but the same capacity which is presently under MTOA will
get converted to LTA. We will therefore, continue to utilize
and seek scheduling of 150 MW in accordance with extant
rules and regulations. Your reliance on Regulation 24 of
the CERC Regulations for connectivity and open access
2009 is, therefore, misplaced and not applicable as there
is neither any relinquishment of the capacity allocated to
us nor will PGCIL suffer any loss as we will continue to
avail open access of 150 MW.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 13 of 18

We would like to draw your kind attention to our earlier
letter dated 30th Oct‟‟15 cited at 6 above under numbered
para 2 our MTOA in existence as on that date of
operationalizing the LTA, may be short closed for the
balance period of grant”. This in our view suffices the
requirement of prior notice for foreclosure of MTOA
especially in the circumstance in the instant case where
the same transaction of dispatch would be converted to
LTA.
In view of the above, it is requested to immediately
operationalize the LTA of 150 MW by closing the
corresponding 150 MW under MTOA.
Further as required by you vide your letter dated 30th
December, 2015 we consent to payment of any
relinquishment of charges as per applicable regulations,
rules and guidelines.”
xi) The grant of MTOA to November, 2013 application and
grant of LTA to December, 2013 application was made
with the consent of the Appellant and with the clear
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 14 of 18

understanding that whenever the LTA got operationalized
for full quantum, the MTOA was to be relinquished along
with payment of relinquishment charges.”
17. Concededly, none of these facts or events referred to in these
Paragraphs of the judgment are related to the review petitioner herein.
These are unique to the appeal filed by GMR Warora. Neither had the
petitioner made any statement in the meeting dated 15.07.2015 that it would
pay relinquishment charges in line with CERC Regulations for
relinquishment of MTOA nor had it sent letter dated 13.01.2016 to PGCIL
giving its consent for payment of relinquishment charges as per applicable
regulations.
18. On the basis of these facts, which relate to GMR Warora alone, this
Tribunal has observed in Paragraph 7(xi) that grant of LTA and MTOA was
made with the consent of the appellant and with clear understanding that
whenever the LTA got operationalized for full quantum, the MTOA was to be
relinquished along with payment of relinquishment charges.
19. It is true that the Paragraphs 7(xii), 7(xiii) and 7(xiv) this Tribunal has
referred to Regulation 24 to say that the Regulation is couched in absolute
terms and does not admit any interpretation which exempts an MTOA
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 15 of 18

customer from payment of relinquishment charges if the capacity covered
under MTOA is utilized for LTA. This, at best, can be construed as an
additional ground for rejection of the prayer of the appellant in the appeal.
20. The fact remains that factual context in which the petitioner had filed
the appeal no.16/2018 as well as the submissions made by its counsel have
been totally overlooked in the “Analysis” part of the judgment under review
and the judgment has been rendered only upon consideration of the facts
involved in appeal no.363/2017. This Tribunal clearly appears to have been
influenced by the facts/circumstances noted in Paragraphs 7(viii) to 7(xi)
which have been extracted hereinabove, in dismissing the appeals.
Undisputedly, these facts/circumstances are nowhere related to the case of
petitioner in appeal no.16/2018.
21. We are, thus, satisfied that a patent and glaring mistake has occurred
in the judgement dated 11.04.2019 which not only undermines its soundness
but also has resulted in serious miscarriage of justice. The error is very
material and stares in the eye, which is not only difficult but impossible to
ignore. This is a fit case in our opinion where the power of review must be
exercised to correct the patent mistake in the judgement under review. There
is no escape from the conclusion that the facts and circumstances upon
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 16 of 18

which the judgement dated 11.04.2019 has been rendered are not borne out
from the record of appeal no.16/2018 and therefore, it needs to be corrected.
22. We may note here that we would be failing in our duties and would be
perpetuating the glaring mistake in case we don’t review the judgement
dated 11.04.2019 by making much needed corrections in it. To rectify in the
compulsion of judicial conscience. In saying so, we derive strength and
support from the wise and inspiring words of Justice Bronson in Pierce Vs.
Delameter 1 NY3 (1847), “a judge ought to be wise enough to know that he
is fallible and therefore ever ready to learn; great and honest enough to
discard all mere pride of opinion and follow truth wherever it may lead; and
courageous enough to acknowledge his errors”.
23. Thus, we have no hesitation acknowledging that this Tribunal has erred
in dismissing the appeal no.16/2018 of the review petitioner vide common
judgment dated 11.04.2019 along with appeal no.363/2017 upon considering
the facts and circumstances related to appeal no.363/2017 alone. The said
judgment dated 11.04.2019 is manifestly based upon misconception of facts
vis-à-vis the review petitioner herein and thus suffers from an error apparent
on the face of record.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.9 of 2019 Page 17 of 18

24. Accordingly, we allow the review petition and set aside the judgment
dated 11.04.2019 qua the review petitioner herein. We make it clear that the
said judgment would remain in force qua M/s GMR Warora, the appellant in
appeal no.363/2017.
25. The appeal no.16/2018 be now listed for hearing on 21.08.2026.
